raw_comment: Some plants and crops really do need the winter to survive/thrive. For example, some need a cold period for seeds to germinate (and some need to have extreme heat, such as a wildfire to germinate). Some need cool weather to do well after the last frost. Some can't deal with high humidity that comes with warmer weather, and will get fungal infections. And some need the cold to kill insect pests to keep from being eaten up over the growing season due to too many insects. Never mind that some beneficial animals and insects need the cold to also survive/thrive (warming climates may help mites on bees survive, creating problems for native bees, as well as honey bees). As a result, the shifting climate will almost certainly make it difficult, if not impossible to grow certain plants, and maybe even cause the extinction of some plants/crops/insects. For example, wild rice and oats do best in cooler climates, both of which are very nutritious, and wild rice is native to North America and an important crop for some Indigenous tribes.

raw_comment:
I noticed that essentially the "bluer" it is the colder the average lowest temperature is, and vice versa with the red. Now, seeing the difference between these two graphs you can easily see that there are less blue areas in the projected map. It is also important to note that the overall movement is north, it seems darker reds come up from the south to move darker blues out of the way and push north. 

I wonder when/if this trends stops. How long would it take (if possible) for the darkest red to completely take over the map? A more reasonable question might be "how long would it take for the blue to be completely pushed off the map?"
I also wonder how telling these maps are to farmers in these areas, could a farmer really tell how well a crop would grow based on lowest winter temperatures?

This has a huge impact on everyone all over the US, and probably the world. If this really is telling of how well crops will grow in certain areas this impacts what type of foods we eat along with whether or not we have food abundance/how much abundance we have. This has a huge impact on our food in general.

A possible title: "will there have to be a great plant migration?"

| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |

raw_comment:
I noticed that while the dark red didn't necessarily increase by a lot, some of the more tan/orange-like colors increased, and the greens and blues decreased a lot up in the north. A good amount of the southeast increased with the second-darkest red, though. 

I wonder if the types of people moving into these areas and the ways the land is being used has affected what the temperature of the area is. I also wonder why the midwest area tended to be less finite in what the color of the area is while in the east, the colors are in rows of a sort. 

This impacts all of us a lot, especially because we could be causing the area to grow hotter. On an average, none of the temperatures got cooler, so we would definitely have to figure out how exactly our actions are affecting the temperatures and how those temperatures are affecting the natural world and its animals. 

A possible headline: "Increasing temperatures are changing plant survival and growth"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the lowest temperature was getting a lot higher. Even though most of the areas still remained below freezing, a lot more became around zero degrees than the more typical -26 degree in graph 1. Something I found interesting was that these were actually the lowest temperatures, not the average. So, in some states, the temperature actually never hits below 0, or even 0 degrees. Because I live in Canada, even in warmer winters we’ve always reached below 0, at least where I live- in the Greater Toronto Area, and even though the southern states are closer to the equator, it is still in North America. So that part was interesting to me.
	While this graph does not directly impact my community, I can draw some conclusions. Temperatures are increasing dramatically, even in places so close to the Arctic, and that can influence plant growing rates. Even though this might not be as applicable in the winter, I can think of the changes which will occur in the summer. Places which were 20 degrees (Celsius) might rise to 25 degrees, and places which were 25 degrees might rise to 30 degrees. So, what does this mean? Many areas, especially on the border, as they are closer to the equator, will become more arid and make for harder plant growth. This is unsettling, as many agricultural products are produced in Ontario; and as already, the growing season is very short.
	
Headline: 
Lows Rise as Temperatures Climb

raw_comment:
I notice that these maps are used by farmers in order to determine which plants will grow best in their region of the nation. The maps show the average low temperatures for different parts of the country. The first graph shows what the average winter lows were between 1981 and 2010. The second graph shows the present low temperatures/ future projections (2011 to 2040).
I wonder how farmers will adapt to these changing conditions. Will farmers be able to keep up as the climate changes? I am worried that this could affect our food supply. Secondly, I wonder how map #2 compares to the previous map we looked at (the one projecting the climate risks in 2040). Finally, how does this impact wildlife? 
This impacts my community because I can see that the climate in my region of the nation has already shifted. Between the first and second map, my region changed from being part of zone 7 to being part of zone 8. This is likely already affecting farmers and wildlife.

The zones in the United States presented in both maps illustrate a growth of certain zones and a decrease in others over time. The key provided indicates that the hardiness zones each represent different temperature ranges of winter lows. From north to south, the numbered zones increase and shift from cooler colors to warmer colors. When comparing the 1981 - 2010 map to the 2011 - 2040 map, I noticed that the zones shift upwards; specifically, less dark green appears in the northernmost regions of the map and more dark red appears in the southernmost regions of the map.

The shift in zones also appears to affect New York, my home state. Zone 8 encroaches on the southernmost part of the state which means that winters in my community will generally only reach lows of about ten to twenty degrees Fahrenheit. Although the lows are still low enough for snowfall, they still trend closer to the freezing point than Zone 7. 

After reviewing all of the graph’s data, I conclude that the graph represents the effect of climate change on American winter seasons.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed was that areas in the south and the west have higher average winter lows than areas in the north. I wonder why areas on the east coast were not as red as those on the west coast (especially in the north).

The second thing I noticed was that the projection has more area that has at least an average winter low of 0. Also, lower zones such as zone 3 and 4 shrank. I wonder how a projection nearly 20 years in the future was created.

Another thing I wonder is how entire ecosystems will be affected by an increase in temperature.

Since I live on the western side of Long Island, the average winter low in my region is expected to increase according to this model. This can mean some crops grown in my region for agricultural purposes might not be as successful as they were before. I wonder what impact this will have economically on my region as well.

A catchy headline for these maps could include “Global warming to blame for higher winter lows?”

## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic choropleth map** of the contiguous United States, shown in **two panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by time period/scenario**: one map for **1971–2000 (Historical)** and one for **2011–2040 (Projected)**.
- No stacking.
- Uses a **shared color legend** for plant hardiness zones / average winter low ranges.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. regions/states) | Spatial | Position on map |
| Plant hardiness zone | Ordinal | Color/hue fill on map; text labels (“Zone 3” … “10”); legend categories |
| Average winter low temperature range | Quantitative (binned into ranges) | Color/hue via legend categories |
| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |
raw_comment:
I notice that the warmer temperatures are mostly in southern & southwestern states from Florida up to California. However, as we move towards the center of the U.S. our temperature becomes dramatically colder. If we compare these two maps we can see that map #1 has a large area that has very low temperatures. In map #2 we see that this cold area is getting smaller, northern states are slowly getting warmer.
 
I wonder if these more central states are much colder because they are not near an ocean to help regulate/distribute their temperature better. This may account for the massive crop fields up north when we don’t see farms at that scale in southern states.
 
Florida’s hot and humid climate makes it ideal for growing many crops. These include citrus, sugarcane, tomatoes, peppers, cotton, and many more. Our most well-known agricultural product is oranges. If we look at how Florida changes in these maps, Florida is actually getting warmer. Map #1 shows most of Florida is around 30 - 40 degrees. However, in map #2 just over half of the state is in the red. This means that Florida got warmer during this period.
 
This graph is showing us the hardiness zones. These 10 zones represent a temperature variation of 10 degrees ranging from 40 degrees to -40 degrees Fahrenheit. This ultimately shows where farmers are more likely to grow crops, and where might produce a large yield.

Will our crops get chopped: Where is the best place for farmers to plant?

raw_comment:
I noticed that this focuses more on how farmers figure out which zones are best for certain crops rather than figuring out how the temperature would affect the whole U.S. And also by looking at both graphs, it seems that the growing zones tend to increase in heat overtime, but not too much to the point where it gets too dry for a state to go into a drought.

This makes me wonder how farmers and home gardeners use these kinds of graphs for when they have different crops for different zones. Then again, they will most likely sell some of the crops that are best for different zones while keeping the rest.

This doesn’t normally impact me personally because we don’t grow produce like we used to, but this does impact the more agricultural parts of the U.S. since Florida is considered in zone 10, which is considered the hottest zone according to the graph. However, that doesn’t mean it’s not safe to plant crops, but rather certain crops might not be able to grow as effectively as others.

The headline I decided to give this article is “Got a lot of seeds, but don’t know where to put them? Well do I have a gift for you?!” because it also acts as a bit of joke infomercial like the ones you’ll likely hear on the TV. However, instead of some home fitness exercise tool or some type of fancy blender, it would just show you the graphs of where you can place certain seeds.

| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |
raw_comment:
I noticed that the zones have shifted noticeably between the first and second graphs. There is also a clear effect of climate change, as there are more red and orange zones in the bottom map than the top map, indicating it has gotten warmer since the 20th-early 21st century. I wonder if the condition changes shown between the graphs can be noticed by people who were alive for both time periods. I also wonder how the temperature changes have affected the agricultural economy.
This graph has a strong impact on me, my community, and everyone in my country because it shows the results of decades of pollution and contribution to climate change. The graph is a sad sign of nearly irreversible damage, and should serve as a wake-up call to the American people to stop contributing to climate change.

A catchy title for the graph would be, "Rapidly Shrinking Growing Zones: Time to Act"

- **Thematic choropleth map** of the contiguous United States, shown in **two panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by time period/scenario**: one map for **1971–2000 (Historical)** and one for **2011–2040 (Projected)**.
- No stacking.
- Uses a **shared color legend** for plant hardiness zones / average winter low ranges.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. regions/states) | Spatial | Position on map |
| Plant hardiness zone | Ordinal | Color/hue fill on map; text labels (“Zone 3” … “10”); legend categories |
| Average winter low temperature range | Quantitative (binned into ranges) | Color/hue via legend categories |
| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |

raw_comment:
On this graph, I noticed that the zones have definitely shifted over the years comparing the top and bottom maps. I also noticed that
climate change is significant at the bottom since there is much more red and orange than before. Also, this is seen up north as well since the temperature zones in green are shrinking. There are a lot more warm tones than cool tones on the present-day map unlike the other. I wonder why some areas such as the great lakes have a tiny rim of orange when the zone is yellow. It also shows that the map has spots of yellow in the orange or dark green spots in the light green. Might this have to do with altitudes? Another thing I question would be if the increase of dark orange in California is the result of the wildfires. 

The impact that this map has on me and my community would be that this map shows us the harsh reality of climate change and how fast it is destroying our planet. Although the progress shown here might seem minimal, I can't imagine what it would look like after 2040. This shows that we must act now and not wait for someone to clean up our mess later. As a community, we must take responsibility for this and help save our planet as much as we possibly can. This will gravely affect farmers and plantations as the climate changes might ruin the production rate and success.

A catchy headline I would use for this graph would be "Will Agriculture Survive or Perish to Hardiness Zones?"

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is the shrinking area of zone three. This area represents colder temperatures, which may have a drastic impact on evergreen forests and their ecosystems. The second thing I notice is the increase of places within zone 10; although the general area of each zone can be expected to fluctuate due to dynamic equilibrium or general climatology, the rapid influx of high heat areas does not appear to change. Third I also notice the impact these changing zones have on America's great plains. The plains make up a large portion of the American farming sector and are essential to the economy. As the temperature changes, so does the precipitation rate, which may bring about changes to soil composition. If climate change continues, land may not just be too hot but too dry or lack nutrients to farm with.   

While some commentators may argue that this is an issue that will have minimal impact on them directly, irrespective of the fact that climate change is a global issue, the potential economic implications of a situation like this can send the American economy spiraling downwards. Farming is a billion-dollar industry that feeds into the shipping and food sales market. These industries have employees, land, etc.; without them, Americans lose jobs and industry. Companies and individuals like to flout proposed climate regulations, but this is a short-sided viewpoint that may spell out tragedy for modern America. 

Headline: The Things We Lost in the Fire

On the other hand, zones 8, 9, and 10 have grown in size to cover more of the United States. In the West, there also seems to be an increase in temperature near California.

However, from 2011 to the prediction during 2040, that region is surrounded by zone 8 and the area itself is in zone 9. This rapid increase in temperature may be harmful during the summer, especially for those without adequate cooling systems. Overheating can potentially become an issue. In addition, this can spoil produce faster, whether they are imports or manufactured/grown here.

| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |
raw_comment:
When first looking at the two graphs and comparing them, the most noticeable thing was how much the zones shifted in the projected outcome. Despite, not being a huge or dramatic shift in zones, the short time span in which this shift is projected to occur is alarming. This then makes me wonder how much the zones will change following the year 2040. Another question also comes to mind, considering that this graph is projecting zone movement from 2011 to 2040, what do these zones look like today in 2021?
This has a huge impact on my community, as it will essentially influence what agricultural products become most available for consumption. Judging from the graph there is probably going to be a rise in products that are grown in warmer climates, meanwhile those that are grown in colder climates will be come harder to obtain. Then of course comes the additional concern of other changes that climate change will bring.
A headline that could describe what is happening in the graph is, "The U.S. becomes warmer and growing zones shift: U.S. citizens might have to consider changing their diets or facing climate change head on."

What do you notice and /or wonder? 
First, I notice that compared to map #1, map #2 shows a huge rise in the temperature of different regions across the U.S. Secondly, I wonder if this increase in temperature is a result of an increase in pollution and overall climate change. Thirdly, I wonder if these rising temperatures will continue to negatively affect crop production in the U.S. and if it might result in food shortages throughout the U.S.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This has a huge impact on my community because climate change can result in many hardships and difficulties that my community will face, such as rising temperatures and limited resources. Not only this, if the temperatures continue to affect the crops grown in the U.S., my community may face food shortages, which is already a struggle for some families.

What's going on in the graph? 
Rising temperatures throughout the U.S. results in rising struggles or risks in the U.S.

In this graph, I notice the zones are shifting upwards, zone 4 shrunk immensely, and zone three is close to being off the map in the predicted graph. I question if this is beneficial or the opposite due to warmer temperatures rising and global warming becoming a growing issue. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This graph concerns me because although warmer climates may be beneficial and needed for the survival of plants, global warming is becoming a growing concern and whether we are able to prevent this in the years to come.

What’s going on in the graph? 
In this graph, they provide the zones throughout the country and their average lowest temperatures in each zone. Since 2011 and their prediction for the years to come, the warmer climates are shifting upwards and colder climates such as zones 3 and 4 are shrinking. A headline for this graph could be “Changes in these zones provide evidence of drastic climate change.”

## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic choropleth map** of the contiguous United States, shown in **two panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by time period/scenario**: one map for **1971–2000 (Historical)** and one for **2011–2040 (Projected)**.
- No stacking.
- Uses a **shared color legend** for plant hardiness zones / average winter low ranges.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. regions/states) | Spatial | Position on map |
| Plant hardiness zone | Ordinal | Color/hue fill on map; text labels (“Zone 3” … “10”); legend categories |
| Average winter low temperature range | Quantitative (binned into ranges) | Color/hue via legend categories |
| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |
raw_comment:
Looking at the change visible from the graph of 1981-2010 to the graph of 2011-2040, it is clear to notice that many of the sections change with the zone 8, 9, and 10 becoming larger and more apparent. It is also noticeable that Zone 3 and 4 seem to decrease considerably. I wonder if these changes can be attributed to climate change, or if there is another pressing issue causing this.

I do not think that this directly has an impact on my community and I, however, I am sure that there might be an indirect impact. One possible way it could impact us is that it might lower the price of fruits and vegetables that are grown in warm weather throughout the year. As the graph is predicting, if zones 8-10 are expanding and covering more area than before, it means higher temperatures which allow for more crops to be grown at this time in the United States. This would lower their prices as we wouldn't have to import as many fruits and vegetables throughout the year as we can grow much of it in our country.

It is quite clear in these graphs that warmer temperatures seem to be "migrating" northward as time goes on. A catchy could be: "Upwards Shifting Growing Zones: What does this mean for us?"

I wonder if that means we will have to abandon some crops we grow in areas where it may not be as hot. Also, will humans be able to adapt after another thousand years?

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs:  “How Global Warming Has Affected Growing Zones” by Simone of Boston; "Warming Across America: Will Our Agriculture Adapt?" by Aeryn of Portland, Oregon; "Climate Change Can Have an Impact on Your Food. Here's How." by Henna of Valley Stream North High School in New York; “How is Global Warming Impacting Plants?” by DeAnthony of A-tech High School in Brooklyn and “Tropical Plants in Traditionally Colder Areas” by Abby and “It’s Getting Hot in Here!” by Emily, both from Iowa.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, April 9 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the maps, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, where spring is finally busting out all over, and Tara Truesdale of Columbia, South Carolina, who lives in a “pollen wonderland” for now.

- **Small multiples / faceting by time period/scenario**: one map for **1971–2000 (Historical)** and one for **2011–2040 (Projected)**.
- No stacking.
- Uses a **shared color legend** for plant hardiness zones / average winter low ranges.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. regions/states) | Spatial | Position on map |
| Plant hardiness zone | Ordinal | Color/hue fill on map; text labels (“Zone 3” … “10”); legend categories |
| Average winter low temperature range | Quantitative (binned into ranges) | Color/hue via legend categories |
| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |

raw_comment: The two graphs present very interesting and noticeable points. Firstly, I noticed the growth of zone 5 into zone 6. Also, I noticed that zone 6 is the growth of zone 6 into zone 7 on the west coast. This made me wonder what effect does climate change and drought have on the changing zones. A title which can be used to describe the graph is "Regional changes in plant growth".

raw_comment:
I noticed that the winter lows in 2011-2040 are on average warmer than the winter lows in 1981-2010. I wonder if that's a good thing and whether it allows for greater success in planting. Will it allow for more northern states to grow crops? Will it reach a point where it's too hot for agriculture in the south? Zones seem to be based on the average winter lows. For example, areas in zone 9 have an average winter low between 20 and 30. I also noticed that the west coast didn't change as dramatically as the rest of the country. I wonder why that is. Eventually, if the warmer temperatures keep progressing in this pattern, will the colder zones essentially "disappear"?

This impacts me and my community because instead of being a yellow zone with average winter lows from 0 to 10, I'm now in an orange zone with average winter lows from 10 to 20. This graph is in support of global warming and its effects. These graphs are also impactful for those who are in teh agricultural field since these temperatures affect plant hardiness.  

A headline could be, "Will Warmer Weather Grow?".

raw_comment:
"How Has Global Warming Affected Growing Zones?"

After examining the graph, our group noticed a number of things such as the zone 3 part of the graph will become nearly eliminated on the 2011-2040 graph. We also noticed that zone 6-10 will take over almost the whole graph in 2011-2040. The West Coast’s growing zones do not change as dramatically as the rest of the growing zones. Also, the zones are relatively evenly distributed in the 1981-2010 graph but in the 2011-2040 graph they become uneven and unpredictable. We wondered some things after looking at the graph, like how this is affecting the crops that grow in the changing areas? Will the crops that grow there now be different in the future? How does this affect the prices of food? We also wondered how this will impact the United States’ food supply and which crops will not be able to be produced in the US in the 2011-2040 graph that were produced in 1981-2010. This graph impacts us and our community as we live in Minnesota, which is in zone 5 of the growing season in the 2011-2040 graph. The average winter lows for this zone are -20 to -10. This tells us that the rise in temperatures when we reach summer can affect plant growth and the economy. Minnesota plays a big role in the agriculture community and the weather is very important in order for the plants to grow.

A possibility of rising sea levels and larger agricultural factors can potentially displace many people and affect the economy. With a rising temperature, it is important to understand what crops can still be planted throughout the year. We would headline this article, “Danger, climate crisis ahead!”

raw_comment: For the graphs displayed some things our group noticed that there is an easily noticeable shift in the color gradient of the first and second graph due to global warming, Between 1981 and 2010 half of Minnesota was a part of zone 3; but between 2011 and 2040 only its most northern areas will be in zone 3. Another is in the 2011-2040 graph, zones 8 and 9 grew larger from the 1981-2010 graph. We wondered what a graph dated before 1981 would look like for the United States? We also wondered what caused the warmer zones to grow larger over the years? Finally, in the far future will we eventually lose the colder zones? In our community, this can impact the amount of crops that farmers are able to grow depending on how suitable the environment is for the plants. This can also impact which plants succeed more than others. If the projected graph is correct, then the 5th zone will eventually be the majority in Minnesota overtaking the 3rd and 4th zone. Eventually, if this is continuous, the United States will slowly all turn darker and warmer for the winter lows. For our catchy headline we chose “The steadily increasing impacts of global warming on agriculture in the U.S.”

raw_comment: We noticed that within the past 10 years, winter temperatures have been getting warmer than they have been from 1981-2010. These temperatures were recorded in growing zones, and much of the American Midwest is used for farmland. We notice that there is a gradual decrease of temperatures as you go more south, this trend is more common in the middle east and eastern part of the country. When you go further in the west the harder splits of colors or temperatures are less common and everything blends together. We wonder how these changes in temperature will affect crop harvests. We also wonder what measures our society will take to prevent these increases in temperatures.The increasing temperatures can have an impact on the crop harvests, since changes in temperature can have devastating effects on crop yields. With less of a harvest, there could be a lack of food which could lead to an increase in produce prices. Our catchy title is “ Warmer winters and failing crops: How climate change can affect harvests”

We notice that the zones go from the north to the south. Each zone is outlined by longitudinal lines. We also notice that the projected map showcases higher temperatures across the board. 

We wonder if farmers use this as a tool to decide which crops to grow. We also wonder how this impacts different fruits and vegetables that are easily available in each zone. This impacts us because we live in Minnesota, so we are in zone 5. This zone is light green. Our winters can be as low as -10 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit. Our community isn’t largely agricultural, so weather doesn’t typically play a large role in our area.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s choropleths (maps with data represented by gradations of color) show the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) growing zones for three time periods:  historical 1971-2000 and 1981-2010 and projected 2011-2040.  How have growing zones and, therefore, climate changed?  What effect does this have on plants and on us?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these maps. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these maps and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next graph on life expectancy will be released by Friday, April 9 with moderation on Wednesday, April 14.

raw_comment:
I first noticed that the zones seem to be in almost a bullseye-like pattern with the center of the bullseye at the uppermost center of the continental US. I also notice that this “bullseye” appears to shift upwards, meaning the areas are projected to get warmer as time progresses. 

I wonder how the change in winter lows will affect crop production. Will this potentially lead to a food crisis? How will this change affect the southern hemisphere? the equator? Is everywhere getting hotter?

My community is largely agricultural, so weather plays a large role in whether the people in my area are successful or not. A change in weather this drastic could potentially be detrimental to our families and economy.

I would title the graph “It’s getting hot in here” to be fun, but still show the projected increase in winter low temperatures.

raw_comment:
When first viewing this graph, I initially noticed how there is a noticeable shift in the color gradient from the first to the second map. It appears that the zones toward the bottom moved northward while zones already in the north (Zones 3 and 4 for example) became much smaller in the map that predicted plant hardiness from years 2011-2040. I also noticed how winter lows appear to have increased in a larger section of the country in the second map. I wonder whether this was predicted due to rising global warming as a result of the greenhouse effect?  

It appears that a portion of Long Island is predicted to be in Zone 9, which would lead to a significant rise in temperature during winter in my community. This would most likely affect plant growth as well for those who grow their own crops or own any livestock, such as farmers. However, New York is comprised of mainly suburban and urban areas, which means plant growth may not be as large of an issue as it would be in other rural states. Regardless, these environmental changes would lead to having much warmer winters, and people who grow any crops or plants may have to find ways to maintain agricultural efficiency in order to continue to provide for themselves.

A catchy headline for this graph could be, "How Rising Temperatures May Affect Agricultural Efficiency in Your State" because the map is primarily indicating how plant growth will be affected by higher winter lows.

raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed when looking at this graph was that there was a clear shift towards warmer winter lows for the projected graph when compared to the historical graph. This can be seen as the colder zones seem to be diminishing while the warmer ones are growing. After noticing that, it made me wonder why this trend was taking place. The first cause that came to mind was global warming, however I am curious as to if there might be other reasons as well. Another thing that seeing this graph made me wonder about was how this temperature shift will affect the growing of crops. Will this cause there to be new staple crops in the United States or will things still be the same? While I do think this shift in temperature is an important event as a whole, I do not think it will make a very large impact in my community. Where I live in New York is not known for its agriculture and thus it will likely not be majorly impacted by the trend shown. Furthermore, it is already fairly cold and I doubt a slight decrease in temperature would have a major impact. Despite that, if it were to have an impact I would hope that it helps raise awareness in my community about the major changes global warming is causing. Because this graph shows the historical vs. projected average winter lows, I think a catchy headline for it would be "A Major Change In Climate: How Is Your Winter Going To Be Affected."

raw_comment:
One big thing I notice is the hardiness zones in the projected graph become higher in temperature and move north. There is more deeper red (Zone 10) in the projected graph in the southern portion than the historical graph. Zone 3 is nearly pushed out of the north by zone 4. A lot of the pockets of the lower zones also disappear in the projected graph (like in the northwestern states and the northeast).
I wonder how this change in zones will affect American agriculture. The zones that hold a lot of agriculture (the midwest and south) seem to continue to increase greatly in temperature. Will this affect agricultural output and the health of crops, as well as soil health? I know the graph shows winter hardiness but a lot of farms continue through the winter for year-round production, and this trend likely continues into the spring and summer.
The area I live in, the PNW, seems to be going into the highest hardiness zones. I know a lot of people have home gardens that continue through the winter and I'd be interested to know how this will affect them as well. I also know a lot of people that enjoy winter sports in the mountains of the PNW, so will this temperature change also change the snowfall we see at higher elevations?
Headline: "Warming Across America: Will Our Agriculture Adapt?"

raw_comment:
I notice that there is more red in the projected than in the historical. Meaning that the country is gradually going to have warmer winters. I wonder if this is due to global warming or if it is something that is naturally occurring. I also notice that the red is concentrated in what seems like the southern and outer sections at the country's edge. raw_comment: I notice that average winter low temperatures are projected to increase from those in 1981 to 2010. This means that in 2011 to 2040, there will be higher winter temperatures. Since plant hardiness refers to how likely plants are to survive in given temperatures, I anticipate plants that are heat-susceptible will have a difficult time surviving in the years to come. I also wonder how this map can be applied to other countries aside from the US. I read an article the other day about how the cherry blossom season in Japan this year is the earliest it has ever been in at least hundreds of years. How will climate change and increased temperatures impact not only their crop production but also their culture? In my community, I see that Long Island's plant hardiness zone will shift from zone 8 to zone 9. This will definitely impact farmers and cultivators in the area, not to mention the drastic zone changes in upstate New York. A headline would be "Which plants would thrive in the shift of the growing zone?"

raw_comment: The graph is representing the growing zones in the United States changing, and it is also showing the changes that affecting which plants can grow successfully by region. I have noticed that the more red the states are the more difficult it is for plants to grow in the northern part of the states. The lighter a color is the easier it is to increase changes in the environment. I wonder is if these shifts are just as noticeable in other parts of the world. An impact this graph has on me and my community is that we can do some research and encourage people to get involved in our environment and our ecosystems. Like many communities, the lack of plants would affect the food storage and the number of crops that can be grown in the United States. People will go hungry and families will have to fend for themselves. Getting many people involved and working together can help control the climate change that is plaguing our planet and essentially save it. The purpose of the map to show the growing zones or hardiness zones for the next two time periods — one historical and one projected. The zones are based on the coldest temperature of the year at each location averaged over a 30-year period. Farmers and home gardeners use the zones on these maps to inform them of which plants will succeed in their area. If I have to write a catchy headline I would call it "The Affect on Climate Change."

raw_comment: This is small but in Zone 3, the temperature is increasing, since most of the dark green is going away, and it is starting to become like Zone 4. Also, Zone 5, seems to have increased in the north which means that Zones like 3 and 4 are starting to change to be -20 to -10 degrees Fahrenheit. I wonder how this map looks as of right now, in 2021 and I want to see if Zone 5 has taken over the upper north since it seems like that is what is happening. Also, I wonder how it is on the East Coast right now because to me it seems like it is getting warmer since we barely had any snow. Furthermore, were in Winter/Spring and we have temperatures such as 60-70 degrees Fahrenheit which to me is summer weather. Building off from what I had previously said the impact that this would have on me is that my state, MA is starting to get warm itself. With temperatures ranging from 60-70 degrees, some weeks and then it seems like we have normal regular Winter/Spring temperatures, it alternates every week. A catchy headline could be “How Global Warming Has affected Growing Zones”.

raw_comment:
Upon a first glance, there is a definite transition between the color gradients present, as though the general pattern would be moving north. A clear diminishing of the green area and the increased prevalence of the red hues can be identified from the original to the recent infographic. I wonder what elements and factors play a role in this agricultural shift of zones. I hypothesize that global warming and general increase of the earth's temperatures may have influenced the following changes in growing zones. 

I live in a more suburban, even urban zone so the agricultural aspect is not very familiar. However, based on my primary hypothesis of climate change impacting the following trends, I do think those effects are to be identified in an urban landscape. The blistering hot summers and sporadic changes in temperatures in a short span of a week may stem from the same causes. However, from a more agricultural aspect, I would assume this would change crop seasons, even advance the projections of seeding and production. 

The graph itself displays a national division based on harsh winter climates, ranging from negative temperatures to 30-40 degrees. Using a color identification system, the graph indicates severities ranging from negative of dark green to the positive highs of a deep red. A catchy headline for this graph would be "The ever changing farming economy of America: how climate change has changed our cultivation?".

raw_comment: These are two graphs detailing the plant hardiness zones by temperature between 1981-2010 and 2011-2040. I notice that the main difference between the top graph and the second one is that the climate is getting hotter, meaning that there is an increase in plant hardiness. I can see that the redder areas are getting even more red and appear to be pushing upwards to the north of the United States. The darker blue and green colors now appear to be faded as temperature are rising. I wonder as to what is the direct cause of the continental US getting hotter. My prediction is that this is the direct result of global warming. This is a known phenomenon that is making the globe warmer and warmer. Although this does allow plants to grow in more areas, it does make originally warm areas even hotter. This increases the risk of drought and fires. This impacts my community in the sense that the second graph predicts Massachusetts to get hotter and transition to a warmer orange color by this graph. Boston is notorious for it's naturally colder weather in the Northeast, and that recognition and way of living that many people here are accustomed to live by are jeopardized by hotter climates. People in my communities will have to adapt to live in warmer climates than anticipated. Catchy headline: "Which areas are getting colder? Warmer?"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the hardiness zones seem to be moving further north as time goes on. It seems to be small, but it also seems to be incremental. Over a few decades, these hardiness zones will probably change drastically. 
          I wonder how this will affect the agriculture farmers produce in those certain regions. Since these growing zones are used by farmers and home gardeners to determine which plants will succeed in their area, I wonder how farmers will react to these zones increasingly increasing in area. The more area of one zone, the more competition of the crops grown by that specific zone. Therefore, there will probably be more competition amongst farmers eventually as the zones shift and farmers have to readjust to what they are growing. I also wonder if climate change will be so drastic that zone 3's and zone 4's climate change to be incorporated into zone 5's and if that leads to the elimination of certain crops being grown in the U.S.
      I think a good headline for this graph would be: "How Climate Change May Impact U.S. Farmers."

- No stacking.
- Uses a **shared color legend** for plant hardiness zones / average winter low ranges.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. regions/states) | Spatial | Position on map |
| Plant hardiness zone | Ordinal | Color/hue fill on map; text labels (“Zone 3” … “10”); legend categories |
| Average winter low temperature range | Quantitative (binned into ranges) | Color/hue via legend categories |
| Time period / scenario (1971–2000 Historical vs 2011–2040 Projected) | Temporal / categorical | Faceting into two separate map panels; panel titles/subtitles |
| State boundaries | Categorical/geographic reference | Boundary lines |

What do you notice?
I notice that the hardiness zones seem to be moving farther north as time goes on. It seems to be by a little bit each year, but because we are looking at 30 year spans, the shifting looks like a lot.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if this is also happening to other continents like Europe or Asia since the North American continent also shares the seasons with these continents, and also if Africa (the lower part) and South America are experiencing somthing similar but with the hardiness zones moving towards the south.
What impact does this have on you and your community?
This would impact the plants my city can grow. I live in a current zone 5, but by 2040 it looks like I will be living in a zone 6 instead.
What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.
Tropical Plants in Traditionally Colder Areas: By 2040, the hardiness zones for each plant will be slightly shifted to the north. This means that places that are in the northern part of the United States will not be able to grow warmer-area plants that they were unable to grow before.
